title: Color and Human Response
key_themes: Color symbolism in ancient civilizations (Egypt, Tibet, China, India, Americas)
Architectural applications of color in ancient structures
Philosophical theories of color (Pythagoras, Aristotle, da Vinci)
Historical medical and healing beliefs about color
Primitive magical beliefs and rituals involving color
Color in human identity and cultural identity
methodology_notes: Narrative historical review drawing on secondary sources including ancient texts, historical accounts, ethnographic observations, and linguistic analysis. No primary empirical research or quantitative data. Sources cited include Hindu Upanishads, Darwin, Herodotus, archaeological findings (Ur ziggurat), religious texts (Quran, Bible, Buddhist texts), classical philosophy (Aristotle, Pliny, Leonardo da Vinci), and anthropological accounts of indigenous practices.
scope_description: Traces color symbolism and human responses to color across recorded history from Hindu Upanishads (~900 BC) through modern times (1976). Covers multiple cultural traditions: Indian, Egyptian, Mesopotamian, Greek, Chinese, Arabic, Jewish, Christian, Islamic, and indigenous American (Navajo, Hopi) and African (Masai, Nandi) cultures.
limitations: Purely historical and cultural documentation; no empirical data
No statistical analysis or experimental validation
No quantitative measures of human response to color
Secondary source synthesis without primary research
Limited to historical records and cultural traditions; cannot establish causal mechanisms
Anecdotal and ethnographic in nature rather than experimental
overall_theory_links: Color symbolism as universal human phenomenon across cultures
Color as mediator of cultural, religious, and philosophical meaning
Historical evolution of color understanding from mysticism to science
Connection between color, emotion, and physiology (Avicenna, Babbitt, modern medicine)
Color language as reflection of cultural values (final section: 'This Colorful Language')

noteworthy_sections.Architecture: Documents use of color in ancient structures (Ur ziggurat ~2300 BC: black, red, blue, gold; Temple of Nebuchadnezzar ~500 BC: colors associated with planets)
noteworthy_sections.Philosophy: Traces evolution of color theory from Pythagoras through Aristotle (color from mixtures of white/black) to Leonardo da Vinci's 6-color system
noteworthy_sections.Religion: Comprehensive documentation of color associations with deities and religious practice across major traditions
noteworthy_sections.Healing: Historical beliefs from Avicenna's Canon of Medicine (temperaments linked to hair color; blue light soothed, red stimulated blood movement) through 19th-century color therapy (Babbitt); notes modern medical application of blue light for neonatal jaundice
noteworthy_sections.Language: Etymology and idiom showing how color words embed cultural psychology (red = passion/danger; blue = sadness; yellow = cowardice/deception; green = jealousy; black = evil; white = purity/honor)

source_quality_indicators.historical_depth: Extensive spanning from ~900 BC to 1976 AD
source_quality_indicators.cultural_breadth: Multiple continents and major world traditions represented
source_quality_indicators.documented_sources: 13 references to primary and secondary historical sources
source_quality_indicators.scholarly_grounding: Draws on established historical scholarship (C. Leonard Woolley, James Fergusson, Darwin, classical texts)

publication_context: Presented at 10th Annual Meeting of Canadian Society for Color, Ottawa, Ontario, May 19, 1982. Published in Color Research & Application, Vol. 8, No. 2, Summer 1983.
author_note: Faber Birren was a prominent color theorist and designer (1900-1988); this article reflects his broad humanistic approach to color across history and culture.
